results.title: The Compute Week Aurel Compute spent this week trying to write down what an hour of compute costs. By Thursday the question had no clean answer. | Alexandre Artus
highlights:
The Compute Week
Aurel Compute spent this week trying to write down what an hour of compute costs. By Thursday the question had no clean answer.
Nebius raised its on-demand rates on 1 October. Its own documentation shows both grids: an H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 an hour. That is still a number you can put in a spreadsheet.
The cheaper line is not. From 8 October, preemptible capacity on those GPU platforms moved to dynamic spot pricing. The documentation lists an H100 floor of $0.79, and the ceiling sits one cent under the on-demand rate, so $4.49. The price can move every fifteen minutes inside that band. A fixed $2.15 became a range of nearly six to one.
To be fair, the floor is well below the old price, and a buyer who sets a cap can do better than before. But it is no longer a figure you can put next to a rival quote, and that is what Aurel Compute has to work around.
The public reference that was meant to fix this has not arrived. CME's compute futures were slated for 5 October. Today the page still reads pending regulatory review, with no quotes and the B200 specification cells blank.
One caveat: these are advertised rates. Long reservations carry discounts, so a large buyer pays less.
Aurel Compute brokers physical capacity, Europe first: racks and hours. No derivatives, strictly neutral intermediary.
If you renewed a GPU contract this quarter, what number did you benchmark against?
Write to Aurel Compute and I will go looking.

results.title: Compute Rents Rose 20% While Model Output Prices Halved · LEARN.INVEST
highlights:
Over the same stretch, the machines that run those models got more expensive. The cloud compute provider Nebius raised on-demand GPU rates from October 1: the H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 an hour and the B300 from $7.85 to $9.50, with increases across the range of 17% to 21%. It was the second rise since May, when the H100 was listed at $2.95.

The two prices move apart because different things set them. GPU rents reflect physical capacity that is currently short. Token prices reflect how model vendors choose to compete. OpenAI cut pricing on its GPT-5.6 Luna line by 80% in late July and the index followed it down. That was a pricing decision, not a drop in cost.

results.title: Nebius GPU Cloud 怎么选？H100、H200、B200、L40S 和 96GB RTX PRO 一次看懂 | 智机玄同
highlights:
Nebius 现在公开了 H100、H200、B200、RTX PRO 6000 和 L40S 的 On-Demand 与 Spot 价格。本文给新手解释两套价格怎么读。

智机玄同发布于 2026年10月9日 3 分钟阅读

资料核查日期： 2026年10月9日。价格、库存和服务商规则可能变化，请以官方页面为准。

文章目录

Nebius 现在的 GPU 产品线已经很完整。

从 48GB 的 L40S，到 80GB H100、141GB H200、180GB B200，再到 96GB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell，都能在官方价格页直接看到。

但第一次看 Nebius 价格表，很容易犯一个错误：

把 On-Demand 和 Preemptible Spot 混成一个价格。

这两种资源不是一回事。

## On-Demand 和 Spot 先分开

On-Demand 可以理解成普通按需实例。你需要时创建，用完释放。

Preemptible Spot 是可抢占实例。价格低很多，但平台可以因为容量和需求把实例回收。

Nebius 当前 Spot 价格还会动态变化，官方说明价格可能随着容量、利用率和用户需求调整，甚至每 15 分钟变化。

所以看到：

> H200 from $0.79 / GPU-hour

不要理解成“H200 的正常固定价就是 $0.79”。

那是 Spot 起价，不是 On-Demand 价格。

## 2026-10-01 起的新 On-Demand 价格

Nebius 官网目前同时显示旧价格和“Effective October 1, 2026”价格。

我们应该看后者。

截至 2026-10-09：

- HGX H100 80GB：$4.50 / GPU 小时
- HGX H200 141GB：$5.40 / GPU 小时
- HGX B200 180GB：$8.50 / GPU 小时
- RTX PRO 6000 96GB：$1.80 / GPU 小时
- L40S + Intel CPU： from $1.55 / GPU 小时
- L40S + AMD CPU： from $1.82 / GPU 小时

这些都是官网公开价快照，实际区域和库存仍然要看控制台。

...

## H100 和 H200 怎么选

H100 80GB 和 H200 141GB 都是 Hopper。

最大的区别是显存。

H200 从 80GB 直接提高到 141GB，并使用 HBM3e。

如果你的任务 80GB 内就能舒服运行，H100 可能更省钱。

如果你经常因为 80GB 不够而量化、切模型、缩上下文，H200 的价值就很明显。

详细可以看 H100 vs H200。

## Nebius 的 B200 适合谁

B200 是 Blackwell 数据中心 GPU，180GB HBM3e。

当前 On-Demand 公开价 $8.50 / GPU 小时。

它不是小白第一次跑 ComfyUI 的合理选择。

更适合：

- 大模型训练；
- 大模型高吞吐推理；
- MoE；
- 多 GPU / 集群；
- 真正能利用 Blackwell FP4 和新 Transformer Engine 的工作负载。

如果只是想“显存比 80GB 大”，H200 或 RTX PRO 6000 也应该一起比较。

results.title: Nebius moves spare GPU hours to spot prices | Wire
highlights:
# Nebius moves spare GPU hours to spot prices from $0.79

Nebius switched its spare GPU hours from a fixed price to live spot pricing on 8 October. An H100 hour now floats between $0.79 and $4.49. Nebius gets paid more when clusters are full. The stuck step is the idle hour, and only the console shows it.

#### Sean

 09 Oct 2026 — 4 min read 

Illustrative image. Nebius H100 preemptible price band from 8 Oct 2026.

`WIRE` · `NEOCLOUDS` · `GLOBAL` · Data as at 9 Oct 2026

Nebius no longer sells its spare GPU hours at a fixed price. Since 8 October 2026, its interruptible (preemptible) GPU hours float. An H100 hour now costs anywhere from $0.79 to $4.49. Until last week it was a flat $2.15. The price moves with how full Nebius's clusters are, and it can change every 15 minutes. On the neocloud model, this is the idle-hour step: Nebius now gets paid more for spare chips when they are scarce, and less when they sit.

## What happened

Nebius, the GPU cloud that rents Nvidia chips by the hour, updated its compute price list for October. Two changes, a week apart:

8 October

Preemptible B300, B200, H200, H100 and RTX PRO 6000 hours move to dynamic spot pricing

Nebius Compute pricing documentation

The band

Floor of $0.79 (H100, H200) or $0.99 (B200, B300). Ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate

Price set by capacity, cluster use, customer demand and pricing preferences

1 October

On-demand rates up 17% to 21%: H100 $3.85 to $4.50, B300 $7.85 to $9.50

This raised the spot ceiling too, since the ceiling tracks on-demand

Who can see the price

Current and past spot prices sit inside the Nebius console, not on a public page

Nebius price page, read 9 Oct 2026

...

A GPU earns money only in the hours someone rents it. An hour nobody buys is gone. Preemptible hours are how a cloud sells chips that would otherwise sit idle. The renter gets a cheap price, and Nebius can take the chip back when a full-price customer wants it.

Under the old fixed price, Nebius got the same $2.15 for a spare H100 hour on a quiet night or a packed afternoon. Now it gets what the hour is worth at that moment.

...

## The second-order read

Who gets paid. Nebius, when its clusters are full. A spare B300 hour that earned a flat $4.30 can now earn up to $9.49. The spot price also points spare chips at whoever values them most.

Who pays. Renters running batch jobs, tests and research on spare time. They used to know their price. Now they carry the price risk, on top of the risk of being kicked off.

Who waits. Buyers who want certainty. Nebius still sells multi-month cluster reservations at up to 35% off on-demand. The new spread makes that commitment look better to a renter.

Stuck step. The idle hour. The spot price now moves with how busy the clusters are, so it is a live gauge of GPU utilization. But Nebius shows it only inside its console. Outside investors can't yet see whether spare hours clear near $0.79 or near $4.49.

## Two cautions

The band is the published range, not what renters actually pay. Nebius has not said where spot prices have traded since 8 October.

Spare hours are a small slice of a GPU cloud's revenue. Most of the money comes from long contracts. This change tells you how Nebius prices its leftovers, not how much it earns.

...

Sources: Nebius, Compute pricing in Nebius AI Cloud, read 9 Oct 2026: from 1 Oct 2026 on-demand H100 $4.50 (was $3.85), H200 $5.40 (was $4.50), B200 $8.50 (was $7.15), B300 $9.50 (was $7.85); from 8 Oct 2026 preemptible pricing for B300, B200, H200, H100 and RTX PRO 6000 switches to dynamic spot pricing, preemptible from $0.79 (H100, H200, RTX PRO 6000) and from $0.99 (B200, B300), previously fixed at $2.15 (H100), $2.45 (H200), $3.95 (B200), $4.30 (B300) and $0.95 (RTX PRO 6000); spot prices can change as often as every 15 minutes and the highest is one cent below the on-demand rate; Nebius price page, read 9 Oct 2026: commitment discounts of up to 35% off on-demand for multi-month cluster reservations, current spot prices shown in the Nebius console; GPU Cloud Advisors, 28 Sep 2026: 1 Oct increase of 17% to 21%. The monthly server cost examples, the ceilings as a multiple of the old price, and the spread are our arithmetic. Not investment advice. Do your own research.

results.title: One H100 hour costs $2.20 Or $12.29... | AionCloud
highlights:
One H100 hour costs $2.20 Or $12.29...

Same chip. Same silicon. Same spec sheet. Published rates, right now:
→ Spot platform: $2.20
→ Neoclouds: $2.49–$3.85
→ CoreWeave / AWS: $6.16–$6.88
→ Big clouds: $10.00–$12.29

That’s a 5x spread for identical hardware.

So what are you actually paying for? Not the chip. You’re paying for where it sits, how it’s packaged, who matched it to your workload, and whether it shows up when you need it. The chip doesn’t set the price. The operation does.

results.title: RunPod Secure Cloud H100 SXM went $3.49 to $3.99, October 8, 2026
highlights:
# RunPod Secure Cloud H100 SXM went $3.49 to $3.99, October 8, 2026

The figure$3.49 RunPod Secure Cloud, NVIDIA H100 SXM, on-demand, the last read before the move · $3.49 per GPU-hour, listed since our first read of 2026-09-06 · read Oct 8, 15:41 UTC · source · live page

Every figure below is a reading this site published - a rate read on a provider's own page, or a value of the index computed from such rates - listed with its source under the text and frozen as of that day: prices move, and a dated piece says what was true on its date. The live tables are linked beside each figure.

RunPod’s Secure Cloud raised 12 of its 29 on-demand GPU rates between our reads of October 8, 2026 at 15:41 and 16:41 UTC. The H100 SXM went from $3.49 to $3.99 a GPU-hour (+14.3%), the B200 from $6.79 to $7.99 (+17.7%) and the H200 from $4.59 to $5.29 (+15.3%). The Community Cloud rates for the same cards did not change in that read: the H100 SXM there stayed at $2.69.

## What moved, and what did not

Each of the 12 rates had been the same in every hourly read since we first read it, between September 6 and September 22, 2026. They all changed in one read, at 16:41:08 UTC on October 8, and the read of 05:41 UTC on October 9 returned the same new figures. At the top of the range the B300 went from $7.89 to $8.99 (+13.9%) and the A100 80GB from $1.59 to $1.79 (+12.6%). Among the smaller cards the RTX 4090 went from $0.74 to $0.89, the RTX 5090 from $0.99 to $1.19, the L4 and the A40 each from $0.49 to $0.59, the RTX PRO 6000 from $2.09 to $2.49, the RTX 6000 Ada from $0.84 to $0.99 and the RTX A6000 from $0.53 to $0.59 - rises between 11.3% and 20.4%.

The other 17 Secure Cloud rates, among them the H100 PCIe, H100 NVL, L40S and MI300X, kept their figures. None of the 35 Community Cloud on-demand rates changed in the same read. On Community Cloud the B200 stayed at $5.98, the H200 at $3.59 and the A100 80GB at $1.19.

The Community Cloud H100 SXM stayed at $2.69 an hour while the Secure Cloud one moved. Over a 730-hour month on one GPU, the Secure Cloud rate went from $2,547.70 ($3.49 × 730) to $2,912.70 ($3.99 × 730).

## Where the new rates sit against the median

Our card pages compare each provider’s cheapest on-demand rate - its rate card - with community capacity and marketplace floors kept out, so RunPod enters them at its Secure Cloud figure. In the build read at 05:41 UTC on October 9, the median of 31 H100 SXM rate cards was $3.54; RunPod’s $3.99 sat above it. The B200 median was $7.17 over 32 rate cards, against RunPod’s $7.99; the H200 median $4.51 over 44, against $5.29. The A100 80GB median was $1.84 over 48 rate cards, and RunPod’s new $1.79 sat just under it.

Both RunPod H100 SXM quotes, Secure and Community, are constituents of the week’s H100 index, so the $3.99 is part of that provisional week. Nothing here is forecast: this is what the two reads returned.

## Who moved the figure

The RunPod parser module was not changed on October 8, and the Community Cloud rates it reads in the same call stayed put, so the change came from RunPod’s side. One detail matters for anyone checking: we read RunPod through its public API, and when we opened runpod.io/pricing at 06:43 UTC on October 9, the page’s own markup still carried the earlier Secure Cloud figure of $3.49 for the H100 SXM. The new rates are what the API returned.

results.title: A New Global Business Case: Neoclouds - by Jai Shekhar
highlights:
In October 2025, on one analyst’s tracking, you could rent an NVIDIA H100, the GPU chip most of today’s AI was built on, on a one-year contract at $1.70 an hour. By August 2026, the same contract would cost $2.60. CoreWeave (welcome to India!) raised prices about 25% across its range in July, reports prior-generation pricing at or above where it was years ago, and calls near-term capacity effectively sold out.

...

NVIDIA invests in its own customers, over $40 billion in stakes in early 2026, and some of that money returns as orders for its chips. However, extra demand lifts the price of an old chip only when supply cannot respond, so the question is why can't supply respond?

Neoclouds: GPUs with the cloud stripped off

The companies renting those chips are called neoclouds, and the whole trick is what they leave out. An H100 on Amazon’s cloud costs roughly $5 to $7 an hour on-demand, whereas the same chip on a neocloud averages about $3.40. Commit for a year, and the neocloud price falls to the $2.60 above.

The gap is the catalogue. Amazon, Microsoft and Google sell computing to every kind of business, so their price carries roughly two hundred other services: databases, security, analytics, billing, the machinery a bank depends on. An AI lab has built its own versions of all of it. What it wants is the bare machine, wiring fast enough that a thousand of them behave as one, and the near-certainty that none falls over mid-run. Selling only those three things is the discount.

...

The market has since moved to $2.60.

results.title: Compute market review: Q1 2026: full report | Rillor
highlights:
- Contract prices rose and capacity sold out. SemiAnalysis's one-year H100 contract index rose from $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, almost 40% [1]. It reported on-demand capacity "sold out across all GPU types" and H100 renewals at the rates signed two to three years earlier [1].
- Posted indexes split. Silicon Data's B200 index ended March 24.4% above its 1 January level, while its hyperscaler H100 index held between $7.40 and $7.52 per GPU-hour from 1 March to 20 April [3, 4].
- Rubin entered production and Blackwell orders continued. NVIDIA said Rubin was in full production in January, reported data center revenue of $62.3 billion for its quarter ended 25 January, and announced a partnership with Meta covering millions of Blackwell and Rubin GPUs [5, 6].
- Memory prices nearly doubled. First-quarter conventional DRAM contract prices rose 93% to 98% from the prior quarter, and DRAM industry revenue reached $97 billion [28]. Meta and Microsoft later cited component pricing when raising 2026 spending plans [25, 26].
- Platforms borrowed; neoclouds refinanced. Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon sold notes and equity-linked securities across the quarter, including a 100-year sterling bond [15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. CoreWeave closed an $8.5 billion loan rated A3 by Moody's, priced at SOFR plus 2.25% for its floating tranche [14].
- Spending plans reset higher. For 2026, Alphabet guided $175 billion to $185 billion, Amazon about $200 billion and Meta $115 billion to $135 billion, against 2025 figures of $91.4 billion, $131.8 billion and $72.2 billion [23, 10, 21].

...

### 1. Contract prices rose and capacity sold out

| Measure | Value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One-year H100 contract, October 2025 low | $1.70 per GPU-hour | [1] |
| One-year H100 contract, late January 2026 | Above $2 per GPU-hour | [1] |
| Change, end of January to mid-to-late February | Up 15% to 20% | [1] |
| One-year H100 contract, March 2026 | $2.35 per GPU-hour, almost 40% above the October low | [1] |
| B200 spot on AWS (p6-b200) | Customers "fighting to pay $14/hr/GPU" | [1] |
| Blackwell lead times | Into June and July 2026 | [1] |

SemiAnalysis launched its one-year H100 rental price index on 2 April 2026. It is built from monthly surveys of more than 100 market participants, including neoclouds, buyers and sellers of compute, reported as a 25th to 75th percentile range, and checked against transaction data and a few transactions SemiAnalysis arranged itself [1]. It targets the contract market, which SemiAnalysis says carries most rental volume on terms of six months or longer and which posted prices often follow with a lag [1].

The same report gave direct availability evidence. It said "On-Demand GPU rental capacity is sold out across all GPU types", that by March it was "increasingly impossible to find any H100s, H200s or B200 rental capacity for any term", and that when it asked for 8 nodes (64 GPUs) of H100 or H200, "half the providers we asked were completely sold out" [1]. Some large neoclouds no longer sold single nodes, and some renters were subletting capacity [1]. Lead times for new Blackwell deployments ran into June and July and, market-wide, "all capacity coming online until August to September 2026 has already been booked" [1].

...

### 2. Posted indexes: B200 moved, hyperscaler H100 did not

| Silicon Data series | Period | Reading | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 index | 1 January | 4.40 | [3] |
| B200 index | 11 January (year-to-date low) | 4.29 | [3] |
| B200 index | February range | 4.41 to 4.71 | [3] |
| B200 index | 25 March (year-to-date high) | 6.11 | [3] |
| B200 index | 30 March | 5.48, up 24.4% from 1 January | [3] |
| B200, all sources | March mean and median | $5.09 and $4.96 per GPU-hour | [3] |
| H100 hyperscaler | March | $7.43 to $7.52 per GPU-hour | [3] |
| H100 neocloud | March | $2.43 to $2.63 per GPU-hour, about 8% higher over the month | [3] |
| H100 hyperscaler | 1 March to 20 April | $7.40 to $7.52; unchanged on 39 of 50 days | [4] |

Silicon Data's B200 index was nearly flat in January and February and rose in March: it averaged 4.66 in the first half of the month and 5.53 in the second, crossing 5.0 on 15 March and 6.0 on 23 March [3]. Its March commentary named four drivers: HBM3e contract price increases passing through to cloud rates after a lag of four to six weeks, NVIDIA's GTC conference, a run of frontier model releases that absorbed idle B200 capacity, and agentic inference demand that is persistent and sensitive to latency [3]. It described the late-March move as "B200-specific", with no spillover into H100 demand [3].

The H100 tiers behaved differently from each other. The hyperscaler series moved about 1% in March with a coefficient of variation of 0.5%, while the neocloud series rose about 8% [3]. Across March and April, Silicon Data placed the hyperscaler tier at about three times the neocloud tier [4]. Its April commentary attributed the hyperscaler tier's stability to enterprise reservations and switching costs [4].

Read together, the two sources show where price discovery happened. Contract prices and neocloud rates rose; hyperscaler list prices for the same GPU did not move. A buyer reading only hyperscaler list prices in this quarter would have seen no change.
